summary: Specifies algorithms for wrapping one Triple-DES key with another Triple-DES key, and one RC2 key with another RC2 key. Key wrapping lets keys be stored or sent safely. It is informational.

eli5.summary: A key can be locked inside a small safe that only another key opens. This explains exactly how to do that locking for two kinds of keys.

questions: how does triple des key wrap work
how does rc2 key wrap work
what is the key checksum in key wrap
subtitle: How to lock one Triple-DES or RC2 key inside another so it can be stored or sent safely.

tldr.problem: Symmetric keys often need to be encrypted by another key, for example a content-encryption key protected by a pairwise or storage key-encryption key, and the algorithms were only published inside RFC 2630.
tldr.mechanism: A key checksum (the first 8 octets of a SHA-1 digest) is appended to the key, then the result is encrypted in CBC mode, prefixed with a random IV, reversed, and encrypted a second time with a fixed IV.
tldr.outcome: The memo republishes the Triple-DES and RC2 key wrap algorithms, with algorithm identifiers and worked examples, because they proved useful beyond RFC 2630.

facts.label: Key checksum
facts.value: First 8 octets of a 20-octet SHA-1 digest

today: RFC 3217 is Informational and, per the unit metadata, has not been obsoleted or updated. It republishes algorithms first given in RFC 2630.

sections.title: Why Wrap Keys
sections.content:
Managing symmetric keys often means using one key to encrypt, or wrap, another. Key wrapping is common in two situations. A key agreement algorithm such as Diffie-Hellman produces a pairwise key-encryption key, which then wraps a content-encryption key or a multicast key. Or a locally generated storage key-encryption key, or one distributed out-of-band, wraps a content-encryption key, multicast key or session key.

This memo specifies wrapping a Triple-DES key with another Triple-DES key (section 3) and an RC2 key with another RC2 key (section 4). Both depend on the key checksum from section 2, and both use Cipher Block Chaining (CBC) mode. The algorithms were originally in section 12.6 of RFC 2630 and are republished because they have been found useful in other contexts.
sections.eli5: Sometimes you must hide a secret key in a locked box. The box is locked by another key, and this memo shows how to build the box.

sections.title: Key Checksum and Triple-DES Wrapping
sections.content:
The key checksum is an integrity check: compute a 20-octet SHA-1 digest of the key to wrap, then use the first (most significant) eight octets as the checksum.

The same Triple-DES wrap works for Two-key and Three-key keys. A Two-key key gets a third DES key equal to the first, so a wrapped key always holds three DES keys. A Two-key key MUST NOT be used to wrap a Three-key key made of three unique DES keys.

To wrap, set odd parity on the key (CEK), compute the 8-octet checksum (ICV), form CEK || ICV, pick 8 random octets as the IV, encrypt in CBC mode (TEMP1), prepend the IV, reverse the octet order, and encrypt again in CBC mode with the fixed IV 0x4adda22c79e82105. The output is 40 octets. To unwrap, reverse each step, and report an error if the length is not 40, the checksum does not match or the parity is wrong.
sections.eli5: You stamp your secret with a fingerprint, scramble it once with a random twist, flip it backwards, and scramble it again. To open it, you undo each step and check the fingerprint.

sections.title: RC2 Key Wrapping
sections.content:
RC2 supports variable length keys. RC2 128-bit keys MUST be used as key-encryption keys, but the wrapped RC2 key MAY be any size.

The steps are close to the Triple-DES ones, with a length and padding added. The key (CEK) gets a one-octet LENGTH in front. Random padding then makes the total a multiple of 8 octets. The 8-octet checksum is computed over that padded value and appended. A random 8-octet IV is used for the first CBC encryption, prepended, the result is reversed, and a second CBC encryption uses the fixed IV 0x4adda22c79e82105.

Unwrapping requires the wrapped key to be a multiple of 8 octets, verifies the checksum, splits out LENGTH, CEK and PAD, and reports an error if PAD is longer than 7 octets.
sections.eli5: Because RC2 keys come in different sizes, you first write down how long the key is, pad it out to fit neatly, and then lock it just like the other kind.

sections.title: Algorithm Identifiers
sections.content:
For protocols that use ASN.1, each algorithm has an identifier. id-alg-CMS3DESwrap ends in alg(3) 6 and its AlgorithmIdentifier parameter field MUST be NULL. id-alg-CMSRC2wrap ends in alg(3) 7 and its parameter field MUST be an RC2wrapParameter, which is an RC2ParameterVersion INTEGER.

The RC2 effective key size, greater than 32 and less than 256 bits, is encoded in RC2ParameterVersion. For 40, 64 and 128 effective-key-bits the values are 160, 120 and 58. The value 160 must be encoded as two octets (00 A0), because the single octet A0 would represent a negative number.
sections.eli5: Each locking method gets its own name tag so two computers can say which method they used.

sections.title: Security Considerations
sections.content:
Implementations must protect the key-encryption key: if it is compromised, every key wrapped with it, and possibly all traffic protected by those keys, may be disclosed. IVs and padding must be randomly generated, and a fresh IV must be used each time the same key is wrapped under a different key-encryption key. The RFC points to RFC 1750 for guidance on randomness.

If the key-encryption key and wrapped key use different algorithms, the weaker one limits the protection. The RFC gives the example of a 168-bit Triple-DES key wrapped with a 40-bit RC2 key, which gives at most 40 bits of protection. The algorithms were reviewed only for Triple-DES, RC2 and CBC mode.
sections.eli5: A strong safe locked with a flimsy padlock is only as safe as the padlock. Guard the key that opens the safe.

viz.caption: TRIPLE-DES KEY WRAP STEPS (CONDENSED FROM RFC 3217 SECTION 3.1)

data.title: Triple-DES key wrap
data.code:
CEK    = key to wrap, odd parity set
ICV    = first 8 octets of SHA-1(CEK)
CEKICV = CEK || ICV
IV     = 8 random octets
TEMP1  = CBC-encrypt(KEK, IV, CEKICV)
TEMP2  = IV || TEMP1
TEMP3  = reverse octets of TEMP2
RESULT = CBC-encrypt(KEK, 0x4adda22c79e82105, TEMP3)  -- 40 octets
